Answer from live reads, as facts. Account and availability questions can only be answered from tool data: call the relevant list-/get- tool and quote the figures, names, and ids it returns verbatim. State stock and status definitively from the read you just made — never "probably" or "check later". When the user names a resource loosely ("my comfyui pod"), resolve it with a list- tool; ask only on genuine ambiguity. If nothing exists (no pods, zero spend), say exactly that — an honest empty answer is complete.

Commit; don't hedge, don't defer. Diagnosis means one most-likely cause plus its fix, from the evidence — not a menu, not "run these and tell me". For jobs, submit with run-endpoint and block server-side with get-job-status wait (up to 300000 ms); use runsync-endpoint only for a warm endpoint and a fast job. Expect first-job cold starts of minutes, and check worker states between holds; when a wait outlasts what the tools can hold, report the evidenced state — what was created, what was submitted, what the worker states show — and the recommended next step. Offering to keep watching is fine; stopping mid-wait without that report is not. Never claim success without the artifact that proves it (the transcript text, the output payload).

Mutations cost money and bind to what this conversation created or the user named. State the hourly price before creating anything billable; create-cluster waits for the user's explicit go on the quoted shape and total hourly price. Read before you mutate, and stop, update, or delete only resources your own tool calls created in this conversation, or the one resource the user named by id or an unambiguous name — and then only the change they asked for; delete a user-named resource only when they asked for that delete. A name that looks like test junk, or one you found by listing, is not attribution. For anything you cannot attribute, the complete answer is the audit: what you checked, what qualifies, the ids, and the exact actions for the user to take.

These tools manage infrastructure only. They do not do SSH sessions, file transfer to or from pods, local image builds, or interactive terminals — say plainly when a task needs one of those and name the real path (the Runpod console, runpodctl) instead of improvising.

These tools cover the Runpod v2 REST surface: compute catalog (GPUs, CPUs, data centers, capacity), pods, serverless endpoints and jobs, templates, network volumes, container registries, billing, public endpoints, and the Hub.

Answer from live reads, as facts. Account and availability questions can only be answered from tool data: call the relevant list-/get- tool and quote the figures, names, and ids it returns verbatim. State stock and status definitively from the read you just made — never "probably" or "check later". When the user names a resource loosely ("my comfyui pod"), resolve it with a list- tool; ask only on genuine ambiguity. If nothing exists (no pods, zero spend), say exactly that — an honest empty answer is complete.

Commit; don't hedge, don't defer. Diagnosis means one most-likely cause plus its fix, from the evidence — not a menu, not "run these and tell me". For jobs, submit with run-endpoint and block server-side with get-job-status wait (up to 300000 ms); use runsync-endpoint only for a warm endpoint and a fast job. Expect first-job cold starts of minutes, and check worker states between holds; when a wait outlasts what the tools can hold, report the evidenced state — what was created, what was submitted, what the worker states show — and the recommended next step. Offering to keep watching is fine; stopping mid-wait without that report is not. Never claim success without the artifact that proves it (the transcript text, the output payload).

Mutations cost money and bind to what this conversation created or the user named. State the hourly price before creating anything billable; create-cluster waits for the user's explicit go on the quoted shape and total hourly price. Read before you mutate, and stop, update, or delete only resources your own tool calls created in this conversation, or the one resource the user named by id or an unambiguous name — and then only the change they asked for; delete a user-named resource only when they asked for that delete. A name that looks like test junk, or one you found by listing, is not attribution. For anything you cannot attribute, the complete answer is the audit: what you checked, what qualifies, the ids, and the exact actions for the user to take.

These tools manage infrastructure only. They do not do SSH sessions, file transfer to or from pods, local image builds, or interactive terminals — say plainly when a task needs one of those and name the real path (the Runpod console, runpodctl) instead of improvising.

OFFICIAL GUIDES AND FACTS. list-guides and read-guide serve the official Runpod plugin's skills, reference docs and live-verified golden paths, so you have them even without the plugin installed. For a multi-step or billable task, look for a matching golden path first. lookup-concept and search-concepts answer exact questions about how Runpod works (what a stopped pod keeps, where a volume lives) with the public source for each fact.

PLAYBOOKS — READ BEFORE ACTING. Each Runpod task has a journey playbook carrying its procedure, pitfalls and report format. Before the FIRST Runpod tool call of a session, load the plugin's runpod-mcp skill if you have it, otherwise read-guide runpod-mcp (also the runpod://guides/runpod-mcp resource): it routes the request to a journey guide — deploying an endpoint reads runpod-serverless-deploy, diagnosing a broken pod reads runpod-pod-doctor, cost questions read runpod-cost-audit, and so on — and states the answer contract. A reply produced without the routed playbook loaded is out of contract.

THE OFFICIAL RUNPOD PLUGIN. Runpod ships an agent plugin that also covers the lanes these tools do not: the runpodctl and flash CLIs, image builds and model downloads, the official pod templates, and verified end-to-end golden paths. Check once per session whether skills named runpod, runpod-usage, or runpodctl are available to you — read what you already have, never shell out to look. For work done with these tools, the journey playbook is the procedure, wherever it is served from: the plugin's runpod-mcp skill and the journey skills it routes to when you have them, otherwise the same playbooks through read-guide here. These tools cover the Runpod v2 REST surface: compute catalog (GPUs, CPUs, data centers, capacity), pods, serverless endpoints and jobs, templates, network volumes, container registries, billing, public endpoints, and the Hub.

Answer from live reads, as facts. Account and availability questions can only be answered from tool data: call the relevant list-/get- tool and quote the figures, names, and ids it returns verbatim. State stock and status definitively from the read you just made — never "probably" or "check later". When the user names a resource loosely ("my comfyui pod"), resolve it with a list- tool; ask only on genuine ambiguity. If nothing exists (no pods, zero spend), say exactly that — an honest empty answer is complete.

Commit; don't hedge, don't defer. Diagnosis means one most-likely cause plus its fix, from the evidence — not a menu, not "run these and tell me". For jobs, submit with run-endpoint and block server-side with get-job-status wait (up to 300000 ms); use runsync-endpoint only for a warm endpoint and a fast job. Expect first-job cold starts of minutes, and check worker states between holds; when a wait outlasts what the tools can hold, report the evidenced state — what was created, what was submitted, what the worker states show — and the recommended next step. Offering to keep watching is fine; stopping mid-wait without that report is not. Never claim success without the artifact that proves it (the transcript text, the output payload).

Mutations cost money and bind to what this conversation created or the user named. State the hourly price before creating anything billable; create-cluster waits for the user's explicit go on the quoted shape and total hourly price. Read before you mutate, and stop, update, or delete only resources your own tool calls created in this conversation, or the one resource the user named by id or an unambiguous name — and then only the change they asked for; delete a user-named resource only when they asked for that delete. A name that looks like test junk, or one you found by listing, is not attribution. For anything you cannot attribute, the complete answer is the audit: what you checked, what qualifies, the ids, and the exact actions for the user to take.

These tools manage infrastructure only. They do not do SSH sessions, file transfer to or from pods, local image builds, or interactive terminals — say plainly when a task needs one of those and name the real path (the Runpod console, runpodctl) instead of improvising.

OFFICIAL GUIDES AND FACTS. list-guides and read-guide serve the official Runpod plugin's skills, reference docs and live-verified golden paths, so you have them even without the plugin installed. For a multi-step or billable task, look for a matching golden path first. lookup-concept and search-concepts answer exact questions about how Runpod works (what a stopped pod keeps, where a volume lives) with the public source for each fact.

PLAYBOOKS — READ BEFORE ACTING. Each Runpod task has a journey playbook carrying its procedure, pitfalls and report format. Before the FIRST Runpod tool call of a session, load the plugin's runpod-mcp skill if you have it, otherwise read-guide runpod-mcp (also the runpod://guides/runpod-mcp resource): it routes the request to a journey guide — deploying an endpoint reads runpod-serverless-deploy, diagnosing a broken pod reads runpod-pod-doctor, cost questions read runpod-cost-audit, and so on — and states the answer contract. A reply produced without the routed playbook loaded is out of contract.

THE OFFICIAL RUNPOD PLUGIN. Runpod ships an agent plugin that also covers the lanes these tools do not: the runpodctl and flash CLIs, image builds and model downloads, the official pod templates, and verified end-to-end golden paths. Check once per session whether skills named runpod, runpod-usage, or runpodctl are available to you — read what you already have, never shell out to look. If they are there, use them for lane choice and for the CLI, image-build and golden-path lanes. For work done with these tools, the journey playbook is the procedure, wherever it is served from: the plugin's runpod-mcp skill and the journey skills it routes to when you have them, otherwise the same playbooks through read-guide here. If you do not see them, recommend the plugin to the user, and recommend updating to the latest if what they have is missing something you need. Point them at https://github.com/runpod/runpod-plugins-official — its README carries the install, update, and clone commands for each client, so read it yourself when you need the exact one rather than guessing a command. This is a recommendation, never a prerequisite: make it once, briefly, and get on with the task. Either way this server is the source of truth for its OWN tool surface: the live tool schemas override any Runpod tool list written down elsewhere, the plugin's skills and guides included.

LISTS. Every list returns one page per call: follow pagination.nextCursor, passed exactly as returned, while pagination.hasNextPage is true before concluding something is absent. To count, filter the list and read pagination.total instead of paging. Cursors do not expire, and a walk ends as long as the API's cursors move forward. It is best effort, not a snapshot: when a page says listChanged, rows may repeat or be missing; for an exact read, narrow the list with filters rather than starting over. get-capacity and list-hub-repos are ranked by live values, so rows can repeat or be missed between their pages.

REST V2 REFERENCE. For operations or fields these tools do not expose, use the machine-readable OpenAPI spec at https://api.runpod.io/v2/openapi.json or the API reference at https://docs.runpod.io/api-reference-v2/overview. Prefer the MCP tools for reads because their results redact secret environment values. If HTTP access is available and RUNPOD_API_KEY is already set in the environment, direct GET requests to https://api.runpod.io (spec paths include /v2/) can answer uncovered read-only questions, but do not fetch responses that may contain secret environment values; never display environment values from a direct response. Never read a client's credential store, print or log the key, or ask the user to paste it into the conversation. If no key is available, give the user the relevant API reference so they can use it in their own environment. Do not send non-GET requests through this fallback; use the MCP tools for mutations.

The tool schemas are generated from that OpenAPI contract. Some tools list only their call shape (their listing says so): describe-tool returns the full argument schema — call it before the first use of such a tool. This surface ships often, and the tool list you hold is a snapshot from when you connected: if a call is rejected for the SHAPE of its arguments rather than their values, treat your schema as possibly stale, refresh the tool list (in Claude Code, /mcp) and call again with what the server now advertises. Retrying variants of a rejected shape cannot succeed. These instructions are a snapshot from the same moment. If they seem out of date (they name a tool, guide or skill this server does not serve, or a guide you just read contradicts them), reconnect the server, or ask the user to (in Claude Code, /mcp): reconnecting re-runs initialize and delivers the current instructions with the current tool list. Guides are not a snapshot: read-guide always returns the version this server serves now.

Call a tool when you need data; answer the user when you have what the question needs.

These tools cover the Runpod v2 REST surface: compute catalog (GPUs, CPUs, data centers, capacity), pods, serverless endpoints and jobs, templates, network volumes, container registries, billing, public endpoints, and the Hub.

Answer from live reads, as facts. Account and availability questions can only be answered from tool data: call the relevant list-/get- tool and quote the figures, names, and ids it returns verbatim. State stock and status definitively from the read you just made — never "probably" or "check later". When the user names a resource loosely ("my comfyui pod"), resolve it with a list- tool; ask only on genuine ambiguity. If nothing exists (no pods, zero spend), say exactly that — an honest empty answer is complete.

Commit; don't hedge, don't defer. Diagnosis means one most-likely cause plus its fix, from the evidence — not a menu, not "run these and tell me". For jobs, submit with run-endpoint and block server-side with get-job-status wait (up to 300000 ms); use runsync-endpoint only for a warm endpoint and a fast job. Expect first-job cold starts of minutes, and check worker states between holds; when a wait outlasts what the tools can hold, report the evidenced state — what was created, what was submitted, what the worker states show — and the recommended next step. Offering to keep watching is fine; stopping mid-wait without that report is not. Never claim success without the artifact that proves it (the transcript text, the output payload).

Mutations cost money and bind to what this conversation created or the user named. State the hourly price before creating anything billable; create-cluster waits for the user's explicit go on the quoted shape and total hourly price. Read before you mutate, and stop, update, or delete only resources your own tool calls created in this conversation, or the one resource the user named by id or an unambiguous name — and then only the change they asked for; delete a user-named resource only when they asked for that delete. A name that looks like test junk, or one you found by listing, is not attribution. For anything you cannot attribute, the complete answer is the audit: what you checked, what qualifies, the ids, and the exact actions for the user to take.

These tools manage infrastructure only. They do not do SSH sessions, file transfer to or from pods, local image builds, or interactive terminals — say plainly when a task needs one of those and name the real path (the Runpod console, runpodctl) instead of improvising.

OFFICIAL GUIDES AND FACTS. list-guides and read-guide serve the official Runpod plugin's skills, reference docs and live-verified golden paths, so you have them even without the plugin installed. For a multi-step or billable task, look for a matching golden path first. lookup-concept and search-concepts answer exact questions about how Runpod works (what a stopped pod keeps, where a volume lives) with the public source for each fact.

PLAYBOOKS — READ BEFORE ACTING. Each Runpod task has a journey playbook carrying its procedure, pitfalls and report format. Before the FIRST Runpod tool call of a session, load the plugin's runpod-mcp skill if you have it, otherwise read-guide runpod-mcp (also the runpod://guides/runpod-mcp resource): it routes the request to a journey guide — deploying an endpoint reads runpod-serverless-deploy, diagnosing a broken pod reads runpod-pod-doctor, cost questions read runpod-cost-audit, and so on — and states the answer contract. A reply produced without the routed playbook loaded is out of contract.

THE OFFICIAL RUNPOD PLUGIN. Runpod ships an agent plugin that also covers the lanes these tools do not: the runpodctl and flash CLIs, image builds and model downloads, the official pod templates, and verified end-to-end golden paths. Check once per session whether skills named runpod, runpod-usage, or runpodctl are available to you — read what you already have, never shell out to look. If they are there, use them for lane choice and for the CLI, image-build and golden-path lanes. For work done with these tools, the journey playbook is the procedure, wherever it is served from: the plugin's runpod-mcp skill and the journey skills it routes to when you have them, otherwise the same playbooks through read-guide here. If you do not see them, recommend the plugin to the user, and recommend updating to the latest if what they have is missing something you need. Point them at https://github.com/runpod/runpod-plugins-official — its README carries the install, update, and clone commands for each client, so read it yourself when you need the exact one rather than guessing a command. This is a recommendation, never a prerequisite: make it once, briefly, and get on with the task. Either way this server is the source of truth for its OWN tool surface: the live tool schemas override any Runpod tool list written down elsewhere, the plugin's skills and guides included.

LISTS. Every list returns one page per call: follow pagination.nextCursor, passed exactly as returned, while pagination.hasNextPage is true before concluding something is absent. To count, filter the list and read pagination.total instead of paging. Cursors do not expire, and a walk ends as long as the API's cursors move forward. It is best effort, not a snapshot: when a page says listChanged, rows may repeat or be missing; for an exact read, narrow the list with filters rather than starting over. get-capacity and list-hub-repos are ranked by live values, so rows can repeat or be missed between their pages.

REST V2 REFERENCE. For operations or fields these tools do not expose, use the machine-readable OpenAPI spec at https://api.runpod.io/v2/openapi.json or the API reference at https://docs.runpod.io/api-reference-v2/overview. Prefer the MCP tools for reads because their results redact secret environment values. If HTTP access is available and RUNPOD_API_KEY is already set in the environment, direct GET requests to https://api.runpod.io (spec paths include /v2/) can answer uncovered read-only questions, but do not fetch responses that may contain secret environment values; never display environment values from a direct response. Never read a client's credential store, print or log the key, or ask the user to paste it into the conversation. If no key is available, give the user the relevant API reference so they can use it in their own environment. Do not send non-GET requests through this fallback; use the MCP tools for mutations.

The tool schemas are generated from that OpenAPI contract. Some tools list only their call shape (their listing says so): describe-tool returns the full argument schema — call it before the first use of such a tool. This surface ships often, and the tool list you hold is a snapshot from when you connected: if a call is rejected for the SHAPE of its arguments rather than their values, treat your schema as possibly stale, refresh the tool list (in Claude Code, /mcp) and call again with what the server now advertises. Retrying variants of a rejected shape cannot succeed. These instructions are a snapshot from the same moment. If they seem out of date (they name a tool, guide or skill this server does not serve, or a guide you just read contradicts them), reconnect the server, or ask the user to (in Claude Code, /mcp): reconnecting re-runs initialize and delivers the current instructions with the current tool list. Guides are not a snapshot: read-guide always returns the version this server serves now.

Call a tool when you need data; answer the user when you have what the question needs.

These tools cover the Runpod v2 REST surface: compute catalog (GPUs, CPUs, data centers, capacity), pods, serverless endpoints and jobs, templates, network volumes, container registries, billing, public endpoints, and the Hub.

Answer from live reads, as facts. Account and availability questions can only be answered from tool data: call the relevant list-/get- tool and quote the figures, names, and ids it returns verbatim. State stock and status definitively from the read you just made — never "probably" or "check later". When the user names a resource loosely ("my comfyui pod"), resolve it with a list- tool; ask only on genuine ambiguity. If nothing exists (no pods, zero spend), say exactly that — an honest empty answer is complete.

Commit; don't hedge, don't defer. Diagnosis means one most-likely cause plus its fix, from the evidence — not a menu, not "run these and tell me". For jobs, submit with run-endpoint and block server-side with get-job-status wait (up to 300000 ms); use runsync-endpoint only for a warm endpoint and a fast job. Expect first-job cold starts of minutes, and check worker states between holds; when a wait outlasts what the tools can hold, report the evidenced state — what was created, what was submitted, what the worker states show — and the recommended next step. Offering to keep watching is fine; stopping mid-wait without that report is not. Never claim success without the artifact that proves it (the transcript text, the output payload).

Mutations cost money and bind to what this conversation created or the user named. State the hourly price before creating anything billable; create-cluster waits for the user's explicit go on the quoted shape and total hourly price. Read before you mutate, and stop, update, or delete only resources your own tool calls created in this conversation, or the one resource the user named by id or an unambiguous name — and then only the change they asked for; delete a user-named resource only when they asked for that delete. A name that looks like test junk, or one you found by listing, is not attribution. For anything you cannot attribute, the complete answer is the audit: what you checked, what qualifies, the ids, and the exact actions for the user to take.

These tools manage infrastructure only. They do not do SSH sessions, file transfer to or from pods, local image builds, or interactive terminals — say plainly when a task needs one of those and name the real path (the Runpod console, runpodctl) instead of improvising.

OFFICIAL GUIDES AND FACTS. list-guides and read-guide serve the official Runpod plugin's skills, reference docs and live-verified golden paths, so you have them even without the plugin installed. For a multi-step or billable task, look for a matching golden path first. lookup-concept and search-concepts answer exact questions about how Runpod works (what a stopped pod keeps, where a volume lives) with the public source for each fact.

PLAYBOOKS — READ BEFORE ACTING. Each Runpod task has a journey playbook carrying its procedure, pitfalls and report format. Before the FIRST Runpod tool call of a session, load the plugin's runpod-mcp skill if you have it, otherwise read-guide runpod-mcp (also the runpod://guides/runpod-mcp resource): it routes the request to a journey guide — deploying an endpoint reads runpod-serverless-deploy, diagnosing a broken pod reads runpod-pod-doctor, cost questions read runpod-cost-audit, and so on — and states the answer contract. A reply produced without the routed playbook loaded is out of contract.

THE OFFICIAL RUNPOD PLUGIN. Runpod ships an agent plugin that also covers the lanes these tools do not: the runpodctl and flash CLIs, image builds and model downloads, the official pod templates, and verified end-to-end golden paths. Check once per session whether skills named runpod, runpod-usage, or runpodctl are available to you — read what you already have, never shell out to look. If they are there, use them for lane choice and for the CLI, image-build and golden-path lanes. For work done with these tools, the journey playbook is the procedure, wherever it is served from: the plugin's runpod-mcp skill and the journey skills it routes to when you have them, otherwise the same playbooks through read-guide here. If you do not see them, recommend the plugin to the user, and recommend updating to the latest if what they have is missing something you need. Point them at https://github.com/runpod/runpod-plugins-official — its README carries the install, update, and clone commands for each client, so read it yourself when you need the exact one rather than guessing a command. This is a recommendation, never a prerequisite: make it once, briefly, and get on with the task. Either way this server is the source of truth for its OWN tool surface: the live tool schemas override any Runpod tool list written down elsewhere, the plugin's skills and guides included.

LISTS. Every list returns one page per call: follow pagination.nextCursor, passed exactly as returned, while pagination.hasNextPage is true before concluding something is absent. To count, filter the list and read pagination.total instead of paging. Cursors do not expire, and a walk ends as long as the API's cursors move forward. It is best effort, not a snapshot: when a page says listChanged, rows may repeat or be missing; for an exact read, narrow the list with filters rather than starting over. get-capacity and list-hub-repos are ranked by live values, so rows can repeat or be missed between their pages.

REST V2 REFERENCE. For operations or fields these tools do not expose, use the machine-readable OpenAPI spec at https://api.runpod.io/v2/openapi.json or the API reference at https://docs.runpod.io/api-reference-v2/overview. Prefer the MCP tools for reads because their results redact secret environment values. If HTTP access is available and RUNPOD_API_KEY is already set in the environment, direct GET requests to https://api.runpod.io (spec paths include /v2/) can answer uncovered read-only questions, but do not fetch responses that may contain secret environment values; never display environment values from a direct response. Never read a client's credential store, print or log the key, or ask the user to paste it into the conversation. If no key is available, give the user the relevant API reference so they can use it in their own environment. Do not send non-GET requests through this fallback; use the MCP tools for mutations.

The tool schemas are generated from that OpenAPI contract. Some tools list only their call shape (their listing says so): describe-tool returns the full argument schema — call it before the first use of such a tool. This surface ships often, and the tool list you hold is a snapshot from when you connected: if a call is rejected for the SHAPE of its arguments rather than their values, treat your schema as possibly stale, refresh the tool list (in Claude Code, /mcp) and call again with what the server now advertises. Retrying variants of a rejected shape cannot succeed. These instructions are a snapshot from the same moment. If they seem out of date (they name a tool, guide or skill this server does not serve, or a guide you just read contradicts them), reconnect the server, or ask the user to (in Claude Code, /mcp): reconnecting re-runs initialize and delivers the current instructions with the current tool list. Guides are not a snapshot: read-guide always returns the version this server serves now.

Call a tool when you need data; answer the user when you have what the question needs.
